body_markdown:
Clark Griswold. Aunt Edna. Samantha Baker. Jake Ryan. Gary Wallace. Steff McKee. And, of course, the one and only Ferris Bueller. All characters created by writer, producer, and director John Hughes, who made some of the most popular and enduring movies of the 1980s. Unlike some of the other movies we celebrate in this issue, in Hughes flicks, cars are not central characters, but they sure are supporting stars.


*Welcome to the[Hagerty Movies and Cars Celebration](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/welcome-to-the-hagerty-movies-and-cars-celebration/) , where we highlight and explore the relationship between[cars and the silver screen](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/movies-and-cars/) .*


We all know about the famous[1961 Ferrari 250 GT California Spider](https://www.hagerty.com/media/entertainment/never-before-seen-shots-of-the-ferrari-stunt-emerge-in-new-book-40-years-after-ferris-buellers-day-off/) that Ferris and friends famously borrow on their day off, and the Family Truckster the Griswold family drives cross-country to Wally World. But even secondary cars, in the background of scenes, are chosen with care and intention and tell us something about the characters and the ’80s worlds they inhabited. Hughes characters, often teens coming of age, lived relatable lives full of angst, joy, disappointment, and lust, with active imaginations,
lofty aspirations, and big fantasies to chase in the fictional Chicago suburb of Shermer, Illinois, where Hughes set no fewer than 16 of his films.


Hughes once remarked to P.J. O’Rourke, his former boss and *National Lampoon* editor-in-chief, that “he knew everyone in Shermer, not just the people in his movies. He knew where they lived and what they did for a living.” From extramarital relations to distant cousins, to their innermost desires, Hughes had his entire make-believe world figured out, down to its cars—specifically the sports cars, usually red.


Was John Hughes a car guy? Sadly, we can’t ask him, because he died in 2009 from a heart attack at the age of 59. From what we can surmise from his celluloid canon, though, Hughes had great car taste, as we will see by diving into some of our favorite Hughes automotive selections—both the dashing leads and the well-cast supporting actors.


### ***


Nick French/Courtesy Everett Collection/Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images


## Starring: 1981 Ferrari 308 GTS


Clark Griswold wants to take his family on vacation, but Hughes has other plans, running his fictional lovable loser up every tree possible. Yet somehow, Chevy Chase as Griswold finds a way down, even if it’s with a dog tearing at his pant leg. Cover girl Christie Brinkley in a Rosso Corsa Ferrari 308 GTS comes closer than dead Aunt Edna strapped to the roof of the Wagon Queen Family Truckster to sidelining Griswold’s family fun quest. Brinkley zooms not only into his rearview but quickly embodies the fantasy of every rosso-blooded American male—at least, the 1980s version. She manages to get Griswold down to his shorts before he’s shocked back to reality by a cold motel pool and his wife interrupting the skinny-dipping session.


Before becoming a screenwriter, Hughes wrote ad copy for famed agency Leo Burnett, then picked up a pen in the late 1970s to write for *National Lampoon* . “He wrote so fast and so well, it was hard for a monthly magazine to keep up with him,” P.J. O’Rourke recalled in a 2015 piece for *The Daily Beast* . The movie, *National Lampoon* ’s *Vacation* , was commissioned from a short fiction story Hughes wrote called “Vacation ’58,” inspired by a childhood family road trip. It starts: “If Dad hadn’t shot Walt Disney in the leg, it would have been our best vacation ever.” Sex jokes and humor as off-color as the Metallic Pea wagon follow the Griswolds from the Midwest to Wally World, an obvious facsimile of Disneyland. And while this movie would never be made in the same way today—it’s kind of a *Blazing Saddles* for the ’80s—laughing out loud at Cousin Dale mistaking the video game *Asteroids* for hemorrhoids will never feel like a crime.


Tom Selleck immortalized the 308 in *Magnum, P.I.* as a symbol of the “Greed is Good” ’80s, but *Vacation* , which came out two years earlier than the popular TV show, also deserves credit for establishing the V-8 coupe as aspirational fodder for the common man. This was the decade when everyone imagined they could be rich. You could easily kid yourself into thinking that both the Ferrari and the model were attainable—if only you weren’t saddled with family responsibilities. We can almost see those gears turning when Chevy Chase’s character first lays eyes on the car and Christie Brinkley.


[https://cdn.emagazines.com/default/National_Lampoon_Vacation_ferrari_scene-EDIT_2f0c265b-1322-4f6f-80f7-fc6e4fdf75ab.mp4](https://cdn.emagazines.com/default/National_Lampoon_Vacation_ferrari_scene-EDIT_2f0c265b-1322-4f6f-80f7-fc6e4fdf75ab.mp4)


**Supporting actor:** *The Wagon Queen Family Truckster is a Ford LTD Country Squire wagon that has been replicated so many times, we’ve seen them at more car shows and auctions than the 308 GTS.*


### ***


Nick French/Everett Collection/Universal Pictures


## Starring: 1983 Porsche 944


“Utterly forgettable.” That’s how 1980s it-girl icon Molly Ringwald, as sophomore Samantha Baker, judges herself in the mirror on the morning of her 16th birthday. Her family agrees she’s forgettable, apparently, as Sam’s day is lost in the hulla-baloo of her older sister’s wedding. “You need 4 inches of bod and a great birthday,” Sam decides while on the phone with a friend. In the film, she gets neither. What she does get is over an hour of awkward teenage pining for Jake Ryan, the hot senior in school, played by a dreamy, spiky-haired Michael Schoeffling. Our man Jake drives an even hotter Guards Red Porsche 944.


The front-engine, rear-wheel-drive sports car was entry-level for the brand at the time and, thus, appropriately attainable for the sweater-vested prep whose rich dad no doubt paid for the car. The 944 was viewed more favorably than the 924 as an attainable but still high-status Porsche. With its red paint and Fuchs wheels, the car enhances Jake’s attractiveness. Not only is he a hunk, but he also comes from a family with means and sophistication. Parents with enough money to buy their son a Porsche, but who are not so ostentatious as to spoil him with a 911.


Jake feels trapped by his vapid, hot blonde girlfriend, and Sam offers the quirky self-effacing substance Ringwald would create in her films time and again, making normal girlies with braces and zero booty feel like the Cinderella story could happen for them. The red 944, with its curvaceous fender flares, serves as Jake’s white horse, and by the end credits, Sam gets successfully swept away from her forgetful family to an unforgettable ending.


[https://cdn.emagazines.com/default/Sixteen_Candles_happy_ending_scene-EDIT1_ee6c5442-30f9-4d59-b90d-e3febc53e549.mp4](https://cdn.emagazines.com/default/Sixteen_Candles_happy_ending_scene-EDIT1_ee6c5442-30f9-4d59-b90d-e3febc53e549.mp4)


**Supporting actor:** *Shout out to the Rolls-Royce Corniche convertible in which Ted makes out with Jake’s prom queen girlfriend. Same with the 1981 Oldsmobile Cutlass, which would have only been four years old when the movie was made and was already chopped up in a pivotale auto shop scene.*


### ***


Nick French/Bonnie Schiffman Photography/Paramount Pictures/Getty Images


## Starring: 1978 Porsche 911 SC


Here, Hughes puts the villain in the red sports car for a change. That’s Steff McKee (James Spader), an unbearable snob whose wealth is advertised by the fetching cherry-red 911 he drives. McKee’s best friend, the similarly affluent Blane McDonough (Andrew McCarthy), pines for Andie Walsh (Molly Ringwald again), a quirky middle-class teen who drives a ratty but fittingly quirky Volkswagen Karmann Ghia. Steff is a duplicitous sort who chides Blane that Andie is beneath his station while simultaneously back-handedly pursuing her via the wealth-and-power dynamic.


Here we see the subtle genius of Hughes’ automotive casting. Whereas the 944 in *16 Candles* quietly communicates wealth and status, the 911 driven by Steff absolutely screams privilege.


The brooding Steff leans coolly on his Guards Red 911, looking down his nose at Andie and her peculiar pink thrifted outfits. But we’re all grown up enough now to know that the high school kid with the $50,000 car ([about $150,000 in today’s money](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/911/1978/1978-porsche-911-sc_3.0?id=aCn1I000000D2cDSAS&condition=concours) ) who’s mean to everyone is just hiding his feelings of jealousy and inadequacy. Blane, our hunky yet human fellow rich kid, sums it up best at the film’s close: “You buy everything, Steff. You couldn’t buy her, though, that’s what’s killing you, isn’t it? That’s it, Steff. She thinks you’re sh*t. And deep down, you know she’s right.” We know Blane’s right, too. The kid with the 911 proves to viewers that he’s petty in Porsche and that money cannot buy happiness. Or the girl.


**Supporting actor:** *Andie’s Karmann Ghia is rattle-can-pink perfection.*


### ***


Nick French/CBS/Paramount Pictures/Getty Images


## Starring: 1961 Ferrari 250 GT California Spider


When it comes to this most famous of Hughes flicks, everyone thinks of one thing: a Ferrari 250 GT California Spider[(actually, a replica)](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/hagerty-magazine/why-hollywoods-most-famous-ferrari-is-a-complete-fake/) catapulting backward into oblivion.


However, the red car from this flick we still fantasize about is not a Ferrari, it’s a German performance sedan. Ferris’s dad, Tom Bueller, played by journeyman actor Lyman Ward, drives a Tornado Red 1985 Audi 5000S Turbo Quattro. Bueller senior is an ad guy in downtown Chicago, just as Hughes was. As a creative executive, he wouldn’t be caught dead driving a Lincoln or even a more conservative Mercedes. Audi was an upstart German performance brand, for people in the know. A car aimed at the sort of enlightened modern man who was emerging in the era. A car for a cool dad. We see this in the scene where Tom finds his supposedly sick but obviously faking it son in bed after the Ferrari plunges to its demise. Bueller senior is no Greatest Generation hardass; he’s more than willing to go along.


Dad’s best quality, though? He doesn’t replace his own son, played by Matthew Broderick, in his heart with a pricey Ferrari, as Ferris’s friend Cameron’s dad does, a fact lost on Ferris until the completion of his masterful story arc.


[https://cdn.emagazines.com/default/Ferris_Bueller_professional_scene-2_cb0ff235-09d0-4f1b-a2b8-e522855932d4.mp4](https://cdn.emagazines.com/default/Ferris_Bueller_professional_scene-2_cb0ff235-09d0-4f1b-a2b8-e522855932d4.mp4)


**Supporting actor:** *Shoutout to the white Pontiac Fiero that Bueller daughter Jeanie (Jennifer Grey) got as a birthday present. Not poor Ferris. “I asked for a car. I got a computer,” he laments. How we miss the days when kids understood wheels were better than screens.*


### ***


Nick French/Courtesy Everett Collection/Paramount Pictures


Hughes is credited for calling *She’s Having a Baby* the most autobiographical of his movies. Jake, an aspiring writer played by Kevin Bacon (the movie star version of Hughes), gets a job in an ad agency, then spends the rest of the movie questioning his choices. Which are to get married young and start a family while putting his desired career of writing books on hold. Not 10 minutes into the film, Jake’s flashy best friend, Davis McDonald, played by Alec Baldwin, gives him an out as they’re dressed in their rented tuxes for Jake’s wedding.


“You don’t have to go through with this. You can walk,” Davis says. “You say the word and we are out of here. Marriage will wait. Time won’t.” The conversation takes place in Davis’s red Jag, a perfect vessel for his live-fast, carefree approach to life. His ’74 E-Type, from the end of the model’s 13-year production run, already looked like an elder statesman in 1988 when this movie hit theaters, but it still oozed timeless class. Hughes perhaps felt the Jag added an unexpected dimension to the best buddy character, who otherwise gives off Lamborghini Countach lady-killer vibes. Jake turns down the offer and embraces adulthood the way Hughes himself did after marrying his high school sweetheart at age 20, then becoming the youngest vice president at ad shop Leo Burnett.


The Jag represents a mirage, an unattainable illusion for both young men. Owning and maintaining a 14-year-old Jaguar was out of reach for an aspiring writer. By the end of the movie, it’s clear that Davis has made the wrong choices: He envies Jake and his settled, stable life. To his credit, Davis knows what road Jake will take from the very beginning: “We can split,” he says from behind the Jag’s wheel, “but you’d be back tomorrow.”


Clearly, Hughes was a gifted ad man. Maybe that’s why selling the fantasy in his movies always came easy for him, even if his pattern repeated itself—often taking shape as a red sports car.


[https://cdn.emagazines.com/default/Shes_Having_a_Baby_jaguar_scene2-2a-2a-2b-2-2_303e54b0-3128-4a10-9803-b6b855bff5f4.mp4](https://cdn.emagazines.com/default/Shes_Having_a_Baby_jaguar_scene2-2a-2a-2b-2-2_303e54b0-3128-4a10-9803-b6b855bff5f4.mp4)


**Supporting actor:** *A red Nissan ZX lurks in the neighbor’s driveway during a weird musical dance number of suburban dads pushing lawn mowers, and Jake takes his bride to the hospital in a silver BMW 325i by the end of the movie. So life doesn’t turn out so bad for the fictional ad guy, either.*
